lead: An open thin-walled beam has a free edge where the shear flow must be zero. Moving along the wall, the shear flow grows because the bending stress changes along the beam. This chapter turns that idea into an integral, then into numbers for I, C, Z and lipped sections. The result gives the shear flow distribution and the shear centre, the point where a load causes no twist. Aircraft stringers, spar booms and fuselage frames are open or partly open sections, so this calculation is used in real stress offices.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for q and the shear centre, and Unit 4 for Ixx, Iyy and Ixy.

sections.h3: From a free edge to a shear flow

blocks.text: Cut the wall at a free edge and measure s along the wall centreline from that edge. Consider a small element of wall of length ds and thickness t. The direct stress σ changes along the beam axis z, so the element is not in equilibrium by itself. A shear flow q must act along the wall to balance the change. For bending about the x axis, dq/ds = −t ∂σ/∂z. With σ = M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> and dM<sub>x</sub>/dz = S<sub>y</sub>, integrate from q = 0 at the free edge.

blocks.where: q is the shear flow (N/mm); S<sub>y</sub> is the shear force parallel to y (N); I<sub>xx</sub> = ∫y² dA is the second moment about the centroidal x axis (mm⁴); t is the wall thickness (mm); y is the distance from the centroidal x axis (mm); s is the distance along the wall from the free edge (mm).

blocks.text: For an unsymmetrical section, the x coordinate also contributes. With centroidal axes, S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub> as shear force components, and D = I<sub>xx</sub>I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>², the same equilibrium gives the general open-section form. The sign of q follows the chosen direction of s. Starting at the other free edge reverses every sign but not the physical distribution.
q = −[(S<sub>x</sub>I<sub>xx</sub> − S<sub>y</sub>I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] ∫ t x ds − [(S<sub>y</sub>I<sub>yy</sub> − S<sub>x</sub>I<sub>xy</sub>)/D] ∫ t y ds
blocks.where: x and y are centroidal coordinates (mm); I<sub>yy</sub> = ∫x² dA (mm⁴); I<sub>xy</sub> = ∫xy dA (mm⁴); D = I<sub>xx</sub>I<sub>yy</sub> − I<sub>xy</sub>² (mm⁸). Each integral runs from the same free edge.

sections.h3: Reading the distribution and finding the shear centre

blocks.text: In a symmetrical I-section under vertical shear, q is zero at both flange tips and largest in the web. A C-section has flange flows in opposite directions; their couple moves the shear centre away from the web. A Z-section is point-symmetric; its shear centre is at the centroid when the flanges are equal, but unequal flanges move it. A lipped channel adds short lips; the lip carries shear flow and shifts the shear centre further. If I<sub>xy</sub> is nonzero, q can change sign along a flange, so a zero inside the wall is not a free edge.

items: Choose one free edge and a positive direction for s. Mark where q = 0.
Compute I<sub>xx</sub>, I<sub>yy</sub> and I<sub>xy</sub> about the centroid.
Integrate along the wall at short intervals, carrying q continuously through corners.
Take moments of the shear flows about a convenient point O: M<sub>O</sub> = ∫(x dF<sub>y</sub> − y dF<sub>x</sub>).
For vertical shear through the shear centre at x = e<sub>x</sub>, set M<sub>O</sub> = S<sub>y</sub>e<sub>x</sub> and solve. For horizontal shear, use the corresponding y equation.

blocks.text: Closed loops cannot start at a free edge. They need a cut and a constant q0 round the loop; this is the method of 5.3.

A real wing section has stringers. Replace each stringer by a boom area Bi at (xi, yi), and let the skin carry only shear. For vertical shear and an open path, add the boom contributions crossed so far. This turns the integral into a short sum and is the form used in wing stress notes. The idealization itself is covered in 5.6.

blocks.where: q<sub>start</sub> is the shear flow at the start of the open path (N/mm); B<sub>i</sub> is the boom area (mm²); y<sub>i</sub> is its centroidal height (mm); the sum is over booms already crossed. For unsymmetrical sections add the x term and use D.

figure.caption: Shear flow q along the wall from the top free edge. It is zero at both free edges, reaches −48.214 N/mm at mid-web, and the vertical shear resultant passes through the centroid, the shear centre at x = 0.

spec.aria: A line plot of shear flow against distance along a Z-section, starting and ending at zero and reaching its largest negative value at mid-web.

examples.question: A Z-section has a top flange 40 mm wide from x = 0 to 40 mm, a bottom flange 40 mm wide from x = −40 to 0, and a web 80 mm deep. All walls are 2 mm thick. It carries a vertical shear force S<sub>y</sub> = 3 kN parallel to the web. Use thin-wall centreline dimensions. Compute the shear flow at 10 mm intervals from the top free edge round the section, sketch the distribution, and find the shear centre position.
steps: Take the origin at the centroid: web mid-height, x = 0, y positive upward. I<sub>xx</sub> = 2×80³/12 + 2×(2×40)×40² = 85 333 + 256 000 = 341 333 mm⁴.

Constants: K<sub>x</sub> = S<sub>y</sub>I<sub>xy</sub>/D = 0.030134, K<sub>y</sub> = S<sub>y</sub>I<sub>yy</sub>/D = 0.020089. At the web top, after the top flange, q<sub>start</sub> = K<sub>x</sub>(1600) − K<sub>y</sub>(3200) = −16.071 N/mm.
Top flange, s from the top tip: q = K<sub>x</sub>(80s − s²) − K<sub>y</sub>(80s). At s = 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 mm: q = 0, 5.022, 4.018, −3.013, −16.071 N/mm.
Bottom flange, s leftward from the web bottom: q = q<sub>start</sub> − K<sub>x</sub>s² + K<sub>y</sub>80s. At s = 10, 20, 30, 40 mm: q = −3.013, 4.018, 5.022, 0 N/mm.

For the top flange ∫q ds = 0; for the bottom flange ∫q ds = 0; the web lies on x = 0. Thus the moment of all shear flows about the centroid is M<sub>q</sub> = 0. For vertical shear through x = e<sub>x</sub>, M<sub>q</sub> = S<sub>y</sub>e<sub>x</sub> = 3000e<sub>x</sub>, so e<sub>x</sub> = 0 mm. Point symmetry gives e<sub>y</sub> = 0.

traps: Making q zero at the first flange tip you draw, not at the actual free edge. For a continuous Z wall the free edges are the two ends of the wall; the web-flange corner is not free.
Dropping I<sub>xy</sub> for a Z or lipped section. A vertical shear then still has an x term, and q can reverse sign along a flange.
Reversing the sign of the integral. q = −(S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>)∫t y ds: if s runs the other way, the sign of q flips. Keep one path and state it.
Using the centroid as the shear centre for every open section. C and lipped sections have offset shear centres.
Mixing units: S in N, t, y and s in mm, I in mm⁴, so q comes in N/mm. Using metres gives a factor-of-1000 error.

quiz.q: Define shear flow q and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: Shear flow is the shear force carried per unit length of wall, q = shear force per length, in N/mm.

quiz.q: Why is q zero at a free edge but not automatically zero at every flange-web corner?
quiz.a: At a free edge there is no adjacent wall to supply shear, so q must start at zero. At a corner the flow is continuous from the previous wall, so q equals the value carried into the corner unless that corner is itself a free edge.

quiz.q: A symmetrical open section has S<sub>y</sub> = 5 kN, I<sub>xx</sub> = 2×10⁶ mm⁴, t = 2 mm, y = 30 mm and s = 20 mm from the free edge. Find q.
Why can an equal-flange Z-section have its shear centre at the centroid while a C-section has it offset?
quiz.a: The equal-flange Z has point symmetry, so the shear flows produce no net moment about the centroid for either principal shear direction. A C-section has no such point symmetry; its flange shear flows form a couple, so the resultant must be offset to avoid twist.

quiz.q: In the worked Z-section, q at the web top is −16.071 N/mm. What is q 20 mm down the web?
In boom idealization, what replaces the integral ∫t y ds?
quiz.a: The integral is replaced by the sum ΣB<sub>i</sub>y<sub>i</sub> over the booms already crossed, where B<sub>i</sub> is boom area and y<sub>i</sub> its centroidal height.

quiz.q: If you start the integration from the opposite free edge of the same open section, what happens to q and to the shear centre?
quiz.a: Every q changes sign because s reverses, but the physical shear flow directions and magnitudes do not change. The shear centre is unchanged.

beyond: Not for the exam. In aircraft stress offices the open-section integral is coded for idealized booms, and the shear centre check is part of every spar and control-surface hinge design. Search for shear centre of Z-section, boom idealization shear flow, and open-section shear flow with unsymmetrical bending. Modern work couples this with Wagner diagonal tension and composite stringers.
